newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: British U.N. envoy calls U.S. arrears "indefensible".
newsitem.headline: British U.N. envoy calls U.S. arrears "indefensible".

text.p: British U.N. envoy Sir John Weston sharply criticised the United States on Thursday for failing to pay its U.N. dues, calling this "indefensible."
"The total owed by Washington is the equivalent of the whole of the U.N. regular budget for one year," he said.
It accounted for two-thirds of the $2.1 billion in U.N. members' arrears for budget dues and peacekeeping costs, he added.
"How can the U.N. put itself to rights in such an ignominious predicament?" Weston asked in unusually pointed criticism of a close ally.

In a speech prepared for a meeting at the United Nations of members of the British-American Chamber of Commerce, he said personal respect and affection for individual American diplomats and public servants "inhibit many in this building from speaking frankly."

"The truth is, failure to pay legal dues is indefensible. It causes great anger and exasperation, even among friends and allies. It poisons the working environment. American exceptionalism cannot mean being the exception to the laws everyone else has to obey. What a reputation to risk, for a nation of such traditional vision and generosity!"

Alluding to repeated U.S. calls for U.N. reform, Weston said if an ailing patient needed surgery, "we would make sure he had normal blood pressure before operating, perhaps even given a quick transfusion," especially if he was expected to return to work next day.

"With the U.N. it seems to be different: the pulse is feeble, blood supply is down, no blood donors in sight. But self-appointed medics pronounce chloroform and the scalpel a cure for overweight. A smarter remedy might be: restore the blood supply to normal, and recommend more exercise."

In his wide-ranging address, Weston speculated about the future of the United Nations in an era of downsized, decentralized governments and a globalized economy, "where it is no longer taken for granted that the nation state within fixed territorial limits is the natural problem-solving unit."
"Fixed bureaucratic hierarchies relying on a formal or physical institutional presence seem old hat. Let's apply this thought to the U.N. system," he said.

"Is there too much bureaucratic hierarchy and not enough fluid and dynamic networking? Is the balance right between inter-governmental activity at the centre and operational services delivered at grassroots in the field?
"Do we spend too much time agonizing over the bureaucrat's favourite pastime of coordination and not enough exposing the different bits of the system to the fresh wind of competition?" he asked.
